design_detail: Brief narrative review (Journal of Psychopharmacology, Reviews section) of how the use of other drugs alongside ecstasy confounds research on MDMA's long-term effects in people, with sections on stimulant amphetamines (neurotoxicity in animals, possible effects in people) and cannabis (psychopathology and cognitive effects in people; neuroprotection at the cellular level and in one rat study). No search strategy, inclusion criteria or quantitative synthesis; 71 references, 6 of them by the authors' group, whose cross-sectional, follow-up and fMRI studies supply much of the human evidence on cannabis co-use. University of Cologne; published 2006.
can_establish: That, by the literature the authors cite up to 2005, most people who use ecstasy also use alcohol, cannabis and stimulants, that many studies compared them with people using no or fewer drugs, and that findings on whether cannabis co-use explains, worsens or offsets problems seen in people who use ecstasy pointed in different directions.
cannot_establish: Whether MDMA, stimulants, cannabis or their combination causes any cognitive or psychiatric outcome in people (the cited human studies are cross-sectional or short follow-ups); whether cannabinoids protect people from MDMA-related harm (the evidence is one rat study, cell studies and a pilot of 8 people per group); or the size of any effect (no pooling or appraisal).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Cited human samples include up to 234 people using ecstasy with other drugs compared with polydrug controls who did not use ecstasy (p. 189); 28 people using ecstasy and cannabis, 28 using cannabis only and 28 using neither (p. 190); 60 abstinent people using ecstasy with other drugs and 30 matched controls, 38 of the former re-examined after 18 months (p. 190); and 8 abstinent people using only MDMA with two matched groups (p. 190).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: None stated; studies chosen by the authors.
sample.attrition: Not applicable. In the cited 18-month follow-up, 38 of 60 people using ecstasy were re-examined (p. 190).
sample.selection_effects: Evidence chosen by the authors. The human studies on cannabis co-use described in most detail are their own (Daumann et al., 2001, 2003, 2004); other groups' contrary findings are cited in one sentence (p. 190). The neuroprotection argument rests on cell studies and one rat study (Morley et al., 2004).

exposure.measurement: Varies across cited studies; mostly self-reported drug histories. The authors note that some earlier studies did not record use of other drugs at all (p. 191).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesized. One cited survey defined novice ecstasy use as a cumulative 1–9 pills (p. 189).
exposure.polysubstance: The topic of the review: the most commonly co-used substances are alcohol, cannabis and stimulants (amphetamines and cocaine) (p. 189).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Described as 'currently abstinent' for the authors' cited studies, without durations in this review.

comparison.controls: As in the cited studies: people who use no drugs, people who use other drugs but not ecstasy, people who use cannabis only, and people using ecstasy without (pure) or with (combined) cannabis and amphetamines.
comparison.matching: The authors' studies are described as using matched controls; matching variables are not given in this review.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The authors note that findings may reflect pre-existing traits of people prone to drug use, or drug use and lifestyle in general (p. 191), and that stimulant-related deficits may reflect low cognitive ability before use (p. 189); no cited human study had measurements before drug use.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: The central issue: polydrug control groups mostly used drugs more moderately than the ecstasy groups (p. 189; p. 191).

outcomes.instruments: As cited: self-reported psychopathology (obsessive-compulsive behaviour, interpersonal sensitivity, depression, anxiety, phobic anxiety, paranoid ideation), memory and learning tests, working-memory fMRI (n-back), PET and SPECT of serotonin and dopamine transporters, PET glucose metabolism, MR spectroscopy; in animals, brain serotonin and 5-HIAA after MDMA with or without cannabinoids.
outcomes.operationalization: Neurotoxicity is framed as loss of serotonergic (and, for stimulants, dopaminergic) axon terminals, transporters and transmitter; functional effects as subtle memory deficits and subclinical psychopathology.

analysis.effect_sizes: None pooled; the review gives prevalence figures and sample sizes but no effect sizes. Co-use: in one survey, everyone new to ecstasy (cumulative 1–9 pills) had smoked cannabis in the previous month and 32% had done so on five or more occasions; earlier studies found 90–100% cannabis co-use (p. 189).
analysis.selective_reporting: Narrative selection. The stimulant section describes neurotoxicity of stimulants alone and offers synergy with MDMA as theory, describing no study of people who combined MDMA with stimulants (an imaging study of amphetamine use among people who use ecstasy is only listed). The authors' own cannabis studies are described in detail, contrary findings in a sentence.
analysis.power: Not applicable; the authors call their fMRI study a small pilot (p. 190).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Most people who use ecstasy also use alcohol, cannabis and stimulants, and many cited studies compared them with people using fewer drugs. Studies with polydrug controls linked raised psychopathology to polydrug use in general rather than to ecstasy; the authors' own studies linked self-reported psychopathology mainly to cannabis, while other groups linked it to ecstasy; cognitive findings were mixed. Cannabinoids partly prevented MDMA-induced serotonin depletion in one rat study; in people, the evidence for an offsetting effect of cannabis is a pilot fMRI study of 8 per group and one study of people using amphetamine-type stimulants.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that cannabis use was shown to contribute to psychological problems and cognitive failures in people who use ecstasy, that cannabinoids were shown to partly block MDMA-induced neurotoxicity in laboratory animals, and that stimulants may act synergistically with MDMA. In the body, the cannabis literature is called inconsistent (p. 190), the stimulant synergy is labelled theoretical (p. 189), and the animal evidence is a single rat study (p. 190). The summary calls reports of residual effects of ecstasy "alarming, although the evidence cannot be considered definite" (p. 191), while also saying the findings may reflect pre-existing traits or polydrug use in general. The abstract's 'shown to contribute' is causal wording for observational associations.

timeline.event: Positron emission tomography study of 15 people abstinent from methamphetamine, cited by this review as Volkow et al. (2001b), where the drug is given as amphetamine; project id volkow_2001a, appraised in the library.

Daumann et al. (authors' group): 28 people using ecstasy and cannabis, 28 using cannabis only and 28 using neither; self-reported subclinical psychopathology mainly associated with extent of cannabis use (as described here).

Daumann et al. (authors' group) fMRI pilot: 8 abstinent people using only MDMA showed lower working-memory activation than non-using controls and/or people also using cannabis and amphetamines; the combined group did not differ from controls (as described here).

Daumann et al. (authors' group): 60 abstinent people using ecstasy with other drugs and 30 matched controls, 38 re-examined after 18 months; psychopathology tracked cannabis rather than MDMA use (as described here).
Morley et al.: in Wistar rats given a neurotoxic MDMA regimen, THC and a synthetic CB1 agonist prevented acute hyperthermia and partly prevented long-term serotonin depletion (as described here).

Halpern et al. recruited people who used ecstasy with minimal exposure to other drugs and alcohol, the design that addresses the confound described here; adjusted differences were small and mostly non-significant across 40 cognitive measures (as summarized on the project's card sc_halpern_2011).

replication.where_it_stands: The confound the review describes is documented and is the reason later studies recruited people with little other drug use (Halpern et al., 2011, in the library). The review's suggestion that cannabis offsets MDMA-related harm in people rests on a rat study, cell studies and a pilot of 8 per group, and has not been tested here in a controlled design; the prospective cohort the authors proposed is not known from this review to have been done.

funding.funder: No funding statement printed in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Psychiatry and Psychotherapy, University of Cologne. The authors wrote 6 of 71 references, including the three human studies behind the cannabis-interaction argument (Daumann et al., 2001, 2003, 2004). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: As the authors propose (p. 191): large prospective cohorts of young people at risk who have not yet used ecstasy, followed for years with recorded drug histories (ideally verified by hair or urine testing) and repeated psychological and cognitive testing; meanwhile, cross-sectional studies that recruit people who used ecstasy with minimal other drug use, or that match controls on the amount of other drugs used, and animal studies at human-relevant doses for interactions between MDMA, stimulants and cannabinoids.

domains.note: No search, dates or criteria; the authors chose the evidence.

No study-by-study appraisal, but the review's subject is a design flaw and it names others (poorly matched controls, earlier studies without data on other drugs, possible pre-existing traits); the authors call their own fMRI study a small pilot.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The human evidence on cannabis co-use described in detail comes from the authors' group (Daumann et al., 2001, 2003, 2004); other groups' contrary findings get a sentence.

The body labels the stimulant synergy theoretical and the protective effect of cannabinoids conceivable, but the abstract turns observational associations into contributions that were shown and gives the rat finding without saying it is a single study.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on whether findings in people who use ecstasy reflect MDMA or other drugs
domains.note: Both directions are cited for cannabis, but the stimulant section presents only harms and a theoretical synergy, describing no study of people who combined MDMA with stimulants; the one described study with a group using MDMA together with amphetamines and cannabis found no difference from non-using controls, which the authors attribute to cannabis rather than weighing it against synergy; and the possible protective role of cannabis receives more space than its evidence base.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist is used, and the overall judgment can be no milder than the worst domain (no systematic search). The review is useful and largely candid about the confound, but its selection is unsystematic and weighted toward the authors' own studies, and the abstract states more than the body. Citable for: how common use of alcohol, cannabis and stimulants is among people who use ecstasy (as summarized from cited surveys), the ways polydrug use confounds studies of MDMA, and the authors' proposal of prospective designs. Not citable for: any causal effect of MDMA, stimulants or cannabis in people, or for cannabinoid protection in people; claims resting on it alone stay at draft and say their figures are second-hand.

key_findings.finding: The authors call the use of other drugs one of the most important confounds in research on people who use ecstasy: the great majority also use other psychoactive drugs, most commonly alcohol, cannabis and stimulants, so comparisons with people who use no drugs cannot isolate MDMA's effects.

In studies with samples of up to 234 people using ecstasy with other drugs and polydrug controls who did not use ecstasy, raised psychopathology appeared to go with polydrug use in general rather than with ecstasy specifically (Parrott et al., 2001; Thomasius et al., 2003; Roiser & Sahakian, 2004); but polydrug control groups mostly used drugs more moderately than the ecstasy groups, which leaves even these comparisons hard to interpret.

Cannabis co-use: in one survey everyone new to ecstasy (cumulative 1–9 pills) had smoked cannabis at least once in the preceding month and 32% on five or more occasions, and more pills went with more frequent cannabis use (Scholey et al., 2004); earlier studies found cannabis co-use in 90–100% of people who use MDMA. Most began cannabis before ecstasy and continued alongside it.

Stimulants: high or repeated doses of amphetamine or methamphetamine damage serotonergic and dopaminergic axon terminals in animal studies; PET and MR spectroscopy studies suggest possible neurotoxicity in people; cross-sectional studies of people using stimulants chronically found deficits in short-term memory, executive control and planning, but whether these are consequences of use or reflect lower ability before use is unclear. The section concludes that co-use of stimulants may enhance MDMA-related serotonergic neurotoxicity and add dopaminergic effects, a synergy the text earlier calls theoretical; the section describes no study of people who combined MDMA with stimulants.
key_findings.locator: Stimulant amphetamines section, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Introduction, 3rd paragraph (theoretical synergy)

key_findings.finding: Cross-sectional study by the authors' group (Daumann et al., 2001): among 28 people using ecstasy and cannabis, 28 using cannabis only and 28 using neither, self-reported subclinical psychopathology was mainly associated with the extent of cannabis use; Morgan et al. (2002) reported similar findings.

Combined cross-sectional and follow-up study by the authors' group (Daumann et al., 2004): 60 currently abstinent people using ecstasy with other drugs and 30 matched controls at baseline, 38 of the 60 re-examined 18 months later; self-reported psychopathology was mainly associated with cannabis rather than MDMA use; those who stopped ecstasy did not differ from those who continued, while those who kept using cannabis regularly reported more problems than those who stopped.
key_findings.note: Whether stopping was chosen or assigned is not stated, so the stop-versus-continue comparison is observational. Editors' arithmetic: 22 of 60 (37%) were not re-examined.

key_findings.finding: Other groups reported clearer associations between psychopathology and the extent of ecstasy rather than cannabis use, or fewer complaints in people using MDMA with cannabis than in those using MDMA alone (Milani et al., 2002; Parrott et al., 2002).

Cognition: several studies related deficits to the extent of MDMA use with little sign of an effect of other drugs; some found an additional effect of cannabis on short- and medium-term memory and learning; a minority found deficits more closely associated with cannabis than with MDMA use in people using both.

In a study of people using amphetamine-type stimulants (Gonzalez et al., 2004), those who also used cannabis showed less cognitive impairment than those who did not; the groups were similar except for more cocaine dependence in the combined group. The authors' fMRI pilot (Daumann et al., 2003) found lower working-memory activation in 8 abstinent people using only MDMA than in matched controls and/or people also using cannabis and amphetamines, while the combined group did not differ from controls; the authors suggest cannabis might offset MDMA-related changes and note that the fMRI literature on cannabis is far from conclusive.
key_findings.note: The review gives the drug in the Gonzalez study as amphetamine; its title in the reference list (p. 191) says methamphetamine. The sizes of the two matched groups in the pilot are not given here.

key_findings.finding: Animal evidence for protection: in Wistar rats given a neurotoxic MDMA regimen, THC and a synthetic CB1 agonist prevented acute hyperthermia and partly prevented the long-term serotonin depletion measured 2 or 7 weeks later; a CB1 antagonist did not block this protection, and the study's authors proposed a CB1-independent, possibly antioxidant mechanism (Morley et al., 2004). Cannabinoids also showed antioxidant and neuroprotective actions in cell and other animal models.
key_findings.locator: Cannabis section, 2nd paragraph (p. 189, continuing on p. 190)

key_findings.finding: Summary: the authors call reports of residual neuropsychiatric effects of ecstasy alarming but not definite; the subtle abnormalities found in cross-sectional studies may reflect serotonergic neurotoxicity but may also reflect pre-existing traits, drug use in general or associated lifestyle; earlier studies often did not record other drugs and many used poorly matched controls. The most consistent finding is a subtle weakening of memory, correlated with the extent of ecstasy use.
key_findings.locator: Summary and perspectives for future research, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Proposed research: since cross-sectional field studies will never be free of the polydrug problem and follow-up studies may not suffice, the authors call for prospective cohorts of young people who do not yet use drugs but belong to risk groups, followed for years with recorded drug histories and repeated psychological and cognitive testing, and for animal studies of drug interactions, especially possible cannabinoid protection.
key_findings.locator: Summary and perspectives for future research, 2nd paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: Three studies of people who used methamphetamine are described in the text as studies of people using amphetamine: Volkow et al. (2001b; 15 abstinent participants), Gonzalez et al. (2004) and Voytek et al. (2005); the titles in the reference list say methamphetamine.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims about amphetamine drawn from this review would rest on methamphetamine studies. The review's Volkow et al. (2001b) is the project's volkow_2001a, and its Volkow et al. (2001a) is the project's volkow_2001c; use the DOI when cross-referencing.

reporting_issues.issue: The description of Volkow et al. (2001b) as showing associations of reduced dopamine transporter density with poorer fine-motor and memory performance does not say that these were correlations within the methamphetamine group, with no comparison of test scores against controls (as the project's card sc_volkow_2001a records).
reporting_issues.consequence: The citation can be read as showing impairment relative to people who do not use the drug, which that study did not test.

reporting_issues.issue: An imaging study cited in the text as Renemann et al. (2002) appears in the reference list as Reneman et al. (2002), titled as a study of amphetamine use by people who use ecstasy and striatal dopamine transporter density; it is listed among stimulant imaging studies, but its findings are not described.
reporting_issues.consequence: The stimulant–MDMA synergy is presented without summarizing the cited study that bears most directly on it; a reader cannot tell from the review what it found.
